issues.legal_issue: A temple manager holding public-purpose land under departmental control cannot transfer the land by lease to a cultivator.
material_facts: The land had been resumed as government property and placed under the control of the department responsible for religious endowments.
The temple priest held and managed the land under a departmental grant for temple worship and upkeep, and could arrange for its cultivation by another person.
The priest granted a cultivation patta to the cultivator.
issues.conclusion: The priest had no authority to lease the land; the patta was invalid and conferred no right or interest on the cultivator.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13 of the Kawaid Maufidaran, section 2(29) of the Qanoon Mal, and the prescribed form of the Parwana show that the priest’s position was that of a manager under the Aukaf Department, not an ordinary tenant with transferable rights. The restrictions on the manager’s rights, including the department’s power to remove him and resume the grant, precluded transfer by lease as well as by sale or mortgage. The Court approved Thakur Panchamsingh v. Mahant Ramkishandas, AIR 1972 MP 14.

predicates.public_purpose_temple_land: The land is set aside for a public purpose connected with a temple.
predicates.manager_holds_for_department: A temple manager holds the land on behalf of a government department and under its control.
predicates.manager_leases_land: The manager grants another person a lease to cultivate the land.

issues.definition: When a manager under departmental control leases public-purpose temple land, the lease creates no right in the cultivator.

issues.legal_issue: A person cannot acquire landholder rights through a tenancy that was never validly created before the relevant statutory transition.
material_facts: The cultivator relied on a patta granted by a temple priest who lacked authority to lease the government-owned temple land.
The cultivator claimed landholder rights on the basis that he was a subtenant when the statutory land code came into force.
issues.conclusion: The cultivator did not acquire Bhumiswami rights because the invalid patta did not make him a subtenant at the relevant time.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 185, 189 and 190 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, the asserted route to Bhumiswami rights depended on the person being an occupancy tenant and on the statutory conditions for conversion being met. Because the invalid patta created no tenancy rights, the cultivator was not a subtenant at the commencement of the Code and could not acquire those rights through that route.

predicates.landholder_rights_claimed_through_tenanc: An occupant claims landholder rights on the basis of a tenancy or subtenancy.
predicates.purported_lessor_lacked_authority: The person who purported to grant the tenancy had no authority to do so.
predicates.no_valid_tenancy_at_transition: The occupant had no valid tenancy when the relevant statutory transition occurred.

issues.definition: A claim to landholder rights through tenancy fails when the purported grantor lacked authority and no valid tenancy existed at the statutory transition.

issues.legal_issue: A manager’s proceedings to eject a person allowed to cultivate departmental temple land require the department’s approval.
material_facts: The land was government property held for temple worship and upkeep under the Aukaf Department’s control and supervision.
The temple manager could arrange for another person to cultivate the land.
The manager initiated proceedings under the land code to eject the cultivator.
issues.conclusion: The manager may initiate proceedings to eject an allowed cultivator only after obtaining the Aukaf Department’s approval.
issues.legal_principle: Because the manager holds the land as government property under the department’s overall control and can be removed for mismanagement, the department must exercise control over the initiation of ejectment proceedings. The Court applied section 248(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, in the context of the manager’s limited authority under section 13 of the Kawaid Maufidaran.

predicates.temple_land_under_departmental_control: A manager holds temple land under a government department’s overall control and supervision.
predicates.manager_allowed_cultivation: The manager has allowed another person to cultivate the land.
predicates.summary_ejectment_proceeding_initiated_b: The manager initiates a summary proceeding to eject the person allowed to cultivate.

issues.definition: When a manager initiates summary ejectment proceedings against an allowed cultivator of departmental temple land, departmental approval is required first.

issues.legal_issue: Heirs continuing in possession after the death of a person whose authority to occupy was personal are in unauthorised possession.
material_facts: The cultivator’s asserted authority to occupy the land was, at most, permission for his own lifetime.
The cultivator died while related proceedings were pending, and his legal representatives remained in possession.
The pending proceeding concerned summary ejectment from land set apart for a special purpose.
issues.conclusion: Any authority to occupy ended on the cultivator’s death, making the legal representatives’ continued possession unauthorised and subject to ejectment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 248(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959 empowered summary ejectment of a person unauthorisedly in possession of qualifying land. The Court could take account of supervening events when deciding an appeal or proceeding, relying on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, 1940 FCR 84, Patterson v. State of Alabama, 294 US 600 (1934), and Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, (1974) 2 SCR 539.

rule.if: summary_ejectment_proceeding and special_purpose_land and authority_personal_to_occupant and occupant_died_during_pending_proceeding and heirs_remained_in_possession

predicates.summary_ejectment_proceeding: The proceeding seeks summary ejectment of an occupant.
predicates.special_purpose_land: The land is set apart for a special public purpose.
predicates.authority_personal_to_occupant: The occupant’s permission to possess the land is personal and does not extend beyond that occupant’s lifetime.
predicates.occupant_died_during_pending_proceeding: The occupant died while the proceeding was pending.
predicates.heirs_remained_in_possession: The occupant’s heirs continued to possess the land after the occupant’s death.

issues.definition: When a personal authority to occupy special-purpose land ends because the occupant dies during a pending summary ejectment proceeding, heirs who remain in possession are in unauthorised possession.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may take account of material events occurring after the decision under review when determining the relief to grant.
material_facts: The cultivator died while the writ petition was pending before the High Court.
The cultivator’s legal representatives continued in possession, although any permission granted to the cultivator was limited to his lifetime.
The death affected whether the continuing possession could be treated as authorised.
issues.conclusion: The Court took account of the death during the pending proceeding and determined the legal effect of the heirs’ continued possession on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court may consider facts and events arising after the decision under review when moulding relief. The Court relied on Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, 1940 FCR 84, Patterson v. State of Alabama, 294 US 600 (1934), and Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, (1974) 2 SCR 539.

predicates.review_proceeding_pending: A review or appellate proceeding remains pending before the court.
predicates.material_event_occurs_after_decision_und: A material fact or event arises after the decision being reviewed.
predicates.event_affects_relief: The later event affects the relief that should be granted.

issues.definition: A reviewing court may consider a later event when a proceeding is pending and the event affects the appropriate relief.

issues.legal_issue: Where the department responsible for temple land must decide whether existing occupants may continue cultivation, they should not be dispossessed before that consideration is completed.
material_facts: The land was government property managed for temple worship and upkeep under the Aukaf Department’s control.
The revenue authority had observed that the manager had not cultivated the land and had no cultivation arrangement, and would likely arrange for someone else to cultivate it.
The Court directed a senior departmental official to consider whether the existing occupants could be permitted to cultivate on revised terms.
issues.conclusion: The department was directed to consider whether the occupants could be permitted to cultivate on suitably revised terms, and they were not to be dispossessed until that consideration was completed.
issues.legal_principle: The manager’s authority to arrange cultivation was subject to the Aukaf Department’s overall control and supervision. In light of that control and the recorded absence of a cultivation arrangement by the manager, the Court directed departmental consideration of continued cultivation and interim protection against dispossession.

predicates.department_controls_public_purpose_land: A government department controls land held for a public purpose.
predicates.current_occupants_cultivate_land: The persons in possession are cultivating the land.
predicates.department_review_of_continued_cultivati: The department has been directed to consider whether the current occupants may continue cultivation.

issues.definition: When the department controlling public-purpose land is considering whether current cultivators may continue, those cultivators are not to be dispossessed before that review is completed.
